intro:
These exercises move from understanding a data contract to defending one under change. The chapter's central claim is that serialization is where a Rust program stops being a closed world of owned values and becomes one participant in a larger system: the moment bytes leave the process, the type layout stops mattering and the agreed external shape takes over. The exercises here exist to make that boundary concrete, first by separating the internal domain model from the wire DTO, then by reading a real versioned envelope, and finally by evolving it without breaking anyone.

The harder exercises target the two places this goes wrong in production. The custom money codec exercise forces correct fractional-digit handling so a contract cannot silently lose cents. The zero-copy and rollout exercises connect Rust's ownership and lifetime rules to operational reality: a borrowed view cannot outlive the buffer it points into, and a compatibility break is a deployment coordination problem, not just a code change. The lab ties it together with a version-tolerant decoder you can run without any crates.

exerciseSolutions.title: Separate the domain model from the wire DTO
exerciseSolutions.solution:
A data contract is the agreed external shape of the bytes that cross a service boundary: the field names, the tagging strategy, the encoding of values, and the rules for what a reader may ignore or default. It is distinct from the in-memory model, which is whatever type layout is cheapest and most precise for the work happening inside the process. The contract is what other deployments depend on; the internal type is a private implementation detail you can change freely as long as the conversion to and from the contract still holds.

Two concrete pressures push the wire shape and the domain shape apart. The first is evolution cadence and compatibility: the wire contract must stay readable by deployments you do not control and cannot redeploy in lockstep, so it changes slowly and only in additive, tolerant ways, while the internal aggregate can be refactored aggressively on every release. The second is representation: a public JSON API wants human-readable, debuggable text (money as a decimal string, timestamps normalized, legacy booleans preserved), whereas the domain wants money as a cheap, exact integer count of cents. Payload size and consumer mix add further divergence, an internal binary stream optimizes for bytes on the wire while a public API optimizes for clarity.

If a single struct serves both the public API and the internal aggregate, every external compromise becomes permanent core debt. A legacy boolean encoding or a decimal money string that one old API needed gets baked into the domain type, and now the precise internal unit is gone forever. Worse, the contract and the model can no longer evolve independently: a change demanded by an external consumer forces a change to the aggregate, and a refactor of the aggregate risks an accidental, silent contract break. Custom representation logic, decimal money text, compact IDs, legacy booleans, normalized timestamps, belongs at the serialization edge in custom serializers or a dedicated DTO, not in the domain type, so the internal unit stays cheap and exact and the conversion is the one explicit place compatibility work lives.
criteria: Defines a contract as the agreed external shape of the bytes, explicitly contrasted with internal type layout.
Names at least two divergent pressures: evolution/compatibility cadence and human readability, plus payload size and consumer mix.
States that custom representation (decimal money, legacy booleans) belongs at the serialization edge, not the domain type.
Explains that coupling lets one old wire compromise contaminate and permanently degrade the core model.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the versioned event envelope
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Serializing the OrderEvent::Created variant with internal tagging produces a JSON object whose discriminant lives in a key inside the same object as the variant's fields. Because the enum is annotated #[serde(tag = "kind", rename_all = "snake_case")], the variant name Created is rendered as "created" and stored under the "kind" key. The whole envelope serializes to schema_version, trace_id (null here), event_id, and the nested payload object; trace_id is None and, depending on the format settings, serializes to null. The payload object is: {"kind":"created","order_id":"ord-7","customer_id":"cust-9","total_cents":4200}.

The internal tag lets a reader dispatch on the variant directly rather than guessing it from which fields happen to be present. Without a tag, a reader would have to infer that an object with order_id, customer_id, and total_cents is a Created event and that one with order_id and an optional reason is a Cancelled event, an inference that is fragile the moment two variants share a field set or a new optional field appears. The explicit "kind":"created" key removes that guessing: deserialization reads the tag, selects the variant, and then maps the remaining fields, which is both unambiguous and stable across additive evolution.

The #[serde(default)] on trace_id means a payload that omits the key entirely deserializes successfully, with trace_id taking Option::default(), which is None, instead of producing a missing-field error. That is exactly the forward-compatibility discipline the chapter prescribes: a reader survives an absent optional field by defaulting it. The version and identity information is carried by two distinct fields: schema_version is the explicit version carrier that makes the contract version visible in the data itself, and event_id is the identity carrier that names this specific event. Keeping both in the stable envelope rather than inside the variant payload means version and identity survive regardless of which event variant is nested inside.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The internally tagged JSON for OrderEvent::Created, with the "kind" discriminant inside the payload object.
criteria: Reconstructed JSON places "kind":"created" inside the payload object alongside order_id, customer_id, and total_cents.
States the tag lets the reader dispatch on the variant without inferring it from which fields are present.
Explains that a missing trace_id deserializes to None via #[serde(default)] rather than failing.
Identifies schema_version as the version carrier and event_id as the identity carrier.

exerciseSolutions.title: Add a forward-compatible optional field
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The additive, compatible move is to add the new field as Option<String> annotated #[serde(default)]. The Option type means "this value may legitimately be absent," and #[serde(default)] tells the deserializer to supply Option::default() (which is None) when the key is missing from the input, rather than raising a missing-field error. That single attribute is what makes the field invisible to existing readers and tolerable to new ones.

With the field present, a new-format envelope sets source_service to Some("checkout") and round-trips it back intact. An old-format JSON string that never mentions source_service deserializes without error into an envelope whose source_service is None. Because Serde, by default, also ignores keys it does not recognize, the reverse direction holds too: an old reader handed a new-format payload that includes source_service simply skips the unknown key and parses the rest. So the new field is survivable in both directions.

This change is purely additive and compatible in both directions, forward and backward. A new reader can consume an old payload (the absent field defaults to None), and an old reader can consume a new payload (the unknown field is ignored). The compatibility comes entirely from reader discipline plus the default: no producer needs to be redeployed first, which is precisely the property that makes additive optional fields safe to roll out without coordination.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Adding an optional source_service field with #[serde(default)]; the old-format payload decodes to None without error.
criteria: The new field is Option<String> annotated #[serde(default)] so a missing key deserializes successfully.
An old-format payload lacking the field decodes into a value with source_service set to None.
A new-format payload sets and recovers Some("checkout") correctly via the round trip.
The change is classified as additive and compatible in both directions (forward: old readers survive new writers; backward: new readers survive old writers), with the reasoning given.

exerciseSolutions.title: Write a money codec that does not lose cents
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The serialize side mirrors the chapter's cents_as_decimal: format the integer cents as a decimal string with exactly two fractional digits using format!("{}.{:02}", value / 100, value % 100). The integer division gives the whole units and the modulo gives the cents, and the {:02} format ensures a value like 5 cents renders as "05", not "5", so 1250 cents always serializes to exactly "12.50".

The deserialize side is where the correctness trap lives. The function splits on the dot, then validates that the fractional part is exactly two characters before parsing. This length check is the whole point: the naive version that simply parses the fractional substring and adds it would read "12.5" as twelve units plus five cents, yielding 1205, and "12.500" as twelve units plus five hundred cents, both silently wrong. By requiring cents.len() == 2, inputs like "12.5" (one digit) and "12.500" (three digits) are rejected with a clear error rather than producing a wrong amount. The whole and fractional parts are parsed as u64 and combined as whole * 100 + frac.

Crucially, every failure path surfaces as a deserialization error, not a panic and not a silently wrong value. A missing dot, a wrong fractional length, or a non-numeric component all return Err via serde::de::Error::custom, so the caller's from_str fails cleanly and the bad amount never enters the system. With this discipline, "12.50" deserializes to 1250 cents and re-serializes back to the identical "12.50", a clean round trip that loses no money.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A money codec that serializes 1250 cents as "12.50" and rejects any input whose fractional part is not exactly two digits.
criteria: Serialization formats 1250 cents as exactly "12.50" via format!("{}.{:02}", ...).
Deserialization rejects a fractional part whose length is not exactly two digits with the cents.len() != 2 check.
"12.50" deserializes to 1250 and re-serializes to the identical "12.50" string.
All parse failures surface as Err through serde::de::Error::custom, never a panic or a wrong value.

exerciseSolutions.title: Fix a borrowed field that escapes its buffer
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The compiler error is a lifetime error: a function that parses a locally owned buffer and returns a struct borrowing from it tries to hand back a reference that outlives the data it points into. The borrowed view, a &str or Cow<'de, str> field, is tied by its lifetime to the input bytes. When the function returns, the local buffer is dropped, so the borrow would dangle. The borrow checker rejects this at compile time: the returned struct's lifetime cannot exceed the lifetime of the buffer it was parsed from, and the buffer's lifetime ends at the function boundary. This is the pure-Rust catch the chapter warns about, zero-copy borrowing is free on a hot path but illegal once the value must outlive its input.

The fix is to decide which fields genuinely need zero-copy borrowing and which must own. On the hot path, internal to the parse, borrowing is fine and cheap; the BorrowedAudit<'a> with &str and Cow<'a, str> fields can be produced and consumed within the scope where the buffer is still alive. But the value that crosses the wider subsystem boundary must own its strings. The clean refactor is a paired owned type, an OwnedAudit with String fields, and a conversion that calls into_owned() on each Cow (or to_string()/to_owned() on each &str). A Cow<'a, str> exposes into_owned() precisely for this: it materializes a borrowed view into an owned String, after which the input buffer can be dropped safely.

The operational rule, in one sentence: borrow while parsing if it reduces copying locally, but own the data once the message crosses a wider subsystem boundary, because a borrowed view cannot outlive the buffer it points into. The hot-path parse may still borrow internally, the conversion to owned happens exactly at the boundary where the buffer is about to be dropped, paying one allocation per escaping string in exchange for a value that is safe to return, store, or send onward.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Borrow on the hot-path parse, then convert to an owned type at the boundary via Cow::into_owned so the buffer can be dropped safely.
criteria: Diagnosis names the buffer-outliving issue: the borrow's lifetime cannot exceed the input buffer's, which is dropped on return.
The refactor produces an owned type (OwnedAudit with String fields) at the boundary so the buffer can be dropped safely.
The hot-path parse still borrows internally (BorrowedAudit with Cow) before converting to owned.
The stated rule distinguishes local parsing (borrow) from values crossing a wider boundary (own).

exerciseSolutions.title: Plan a mixed-version producer-consumer rollout
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The rollout order is reader-first, because the safe moves are the ones an old reader can survive without being redeployed. Deploy the tolerant consumers before any producer emits the new shape. A tolerant consumer understands both the old and new field names and defaults the new field when it is absent, so during the window where some producers still emit the old shape and some emit the new one, every consumer can parse every live message. Only after all consumers are upgraded do you begin rolling producers to the new shape. At no instant does a live message reach a reader that cannot parse it, because the readers learned the new vocabulary first. Reversing the order, shipping producers first, guarantees a window where new-shape messages hit old consumers that reject them.

A field rename is made safe by retaining a deprecated alias during the drain window rather than renaming in place. The consumer is taught to read both the new name and the old name (in Serde, #[serde(alias = "old_name")] on the renamed field), so it accepts messages from both old producers, which still emit the old name, and new producers, which emit the new one. The alias stays in place until every old producer has been drained and redeployed; only once no producer emits the old name is it safe to delete the alias. A rename without the alias is an instant break, the new consumer cannot find the field an old producer is still sending.

The version boundary must be made visible in data, tests, and logs before mixed versions meet, because the most expensive serialization bug is silent contract drift that still compiles and deploys. Bump schema_version in the data so a consumer (and a human reading logs) can see which contract a message claims; add tests that decode both an old-shape and a new-shape payload, asserting the alias and the defaulted field both work; and log the observed schema_version distribution so the team can confirm old producers are actually drained before deleting the alias. Finally, route all of this through an explicit DTO-to-domain conversion layer: the wire DTO carries the alias and the optional field, the conversion translates it into the clean domain type, and the domain type never learns about the rename. That separation contains the blast radius, the compatibility shims live in one conversion function, the domain stays clean, and one old wire compromise cannot contaminate the core model.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A tolerant wire DTO with a deprecated alias and a defaulted new field, converted through one explicit layer into a clean domain type.
criteria: The plan deploys tolerant readers before producers emit the new shape, so old and new coexist with no unparseable message.
The rename keeps a deprecated alias (#[serde(alias = "total")]) readable until old producers are fully drained.
The version boundary is surfaced in data (schema_version), tests (decode both shapes), and logs before rollout.
Compatibility work is routed through an explicit DTO-to-domain conversion so the domain type stays clean.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
v2 currency = EUR
v2 round trip ok = true
v1 schema = 1
v1 currency = USD
v1 total cents = 999
labSolution.explanation:
The lab models version-tolerant decoding with no external crates: a payload is a semicolon-separated list of key=value fields, and the decoder is the tolerant reader the chapter prescribes. The completed match arm assigns each recognized key to its field, parsing schema_version and total_cents as numbers and copying the two string fields. The decisive detail is that currency is initialized to a default of "USD" as a mutable binding before the loop, so a payload that omits the currency field leaves the default in place. This is the forward-compatibility rule in plain Rust: a v2 reader supplies a default for a field that v1 writers never emit.

The two backward-compatibility behaviors both fall out of the match. The catch-all arm `_ => {}` silently ignores any key the reader does not recognize, so the v1 payload's unknown `region=eu` field is skipped rather than treated as an error. And because the loop only overwrites a field when its key actually appears, an absent field keeps its initialized value. The v2 round trip therefore reconstructs an identical Record (round_trip == v2 is true), proving encode and decode are inverses for a complete payload.

The printed output follows directly. The v2 case sets currency to EUR and round-trips exactly, printing the EUR line and true. The v1 payload sets schema_version to 1 and total_cents to 999, never mentions currency (so it stays USD), and carries an unknown region field that is dropped. The five lines printed are exactly the expected output: a new reader consuming an old payload, defaulting the new field and ignoring the unrecognized one.

reviewAnswers.question: Which schema changes are invisible to an existing reader, and which require the reader to be redeployed first?
reviewAnswers.answer: Additive changes are invisible to an existing reader: adding an optional field with a default, since old readers ignore the new key and new readers default it when absent. Adding optional fields is safe for a tolerant reader because serde's default behaviour is to skip keys it does not recognize. Changes that require the reader to be redeployed first are the breaking ones: renaming or removing a field without a retained alias, changing a field's type or encoding, or tightening a previously optional field into a required one. The rule is that the safe moves are the ones an old reader can survive without being redeployed, so anything an old reader cannot survive must be preceded by deploying a tolerant reader.

reviewAnswers.question: What does internal enum tagging (#[serde(tag = "kind")]) give a reader that field-shape inference does not?
reviewAnswers.answer: Internal tagging stores the variant discriminant explicitly in a key inside the same object, so the reader dispatches on the variant by reading the tag rather than guessing it from which fields happen to be present. Field-shape inference is fragile: it breaks the moment two variants share a field set or a new optional field shifts the apparent shape, and it forces the reader to encode brittle assumptions about presence. The explicit tag makes deserialization unambiguous and stable across additive evolution, the reader selects the variant from the tag and then maps the remaining fields.

reviewAnswers.question: Why must a borrowed &str or Cow<'de, str> field not outlive the input buffer it was parsed from?
reviewAnswers.answer: A borrowed &str or Cow<'de, str> points directly into the input bytes instead of owning a copy, so its lifetime is chained to that buffer. If the value outlived the buffer, the reference would dangle, pointing at freed memory, which Rust's borrow checker forbids at compile time. This is why a function that drops its buffer on return cannot hand back a struct that borrows from it. The operational rule is to borrow while parsing if it reduces copying locally, but call into_owned() or otherwise own the strings before the value crosses a wider subsystem boundary where the buffer is gone.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is split-on-dot money parsing a correctness trap, and what validation prevents silently losing cents?
reviewAnswers.answer: Splitting on the dot and parsing the fractional part without checking its length silently mis-scales the amount: a reader that accepts "12.5" as five cents reads 1205, and "12.500" as five hundred cents, both wrong, and the error is silent because the parse still succeeds. The fix is to validate that the fractional part is exactly two digits (cents.len() == 2) before combining it as whole * 100 + frac, or to scale by its actual length. Inputs with the wrong fractional length must be rejected with a deserialization error rather than coerced, so a malformed amount fails loudly instead of entering the system as a wrong value.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is a compatibility break a deployment coordination problem rather than only a code change?
reviewAnswers.answer: Producers and consumers deploy on independent schedules, so at any instant during a rollout an old producer may send to a new consumer or the reverse, and a single struct edit that compiles cleanly can still break a live message in that mixed window. The break is therefore about ordering deployments and draining old versions, deploy tolerant readers first, keep deprecated aliases until old producers are gone, and make the version boundary visible in data, tests, and logs, not just about writing correct code. The most expensive serialization bug is silent contract drift that still compiles and deploys and only surfaces when mixed versions meet, which is exactly the failure a coordination plan exists to prevent.

reviewAnswers.question: Why must you never let Rust's in-memory struct layout serve as an FFI contract by default, and what are the two safe alternatives?
reviewAnswers.answer: A plain Rust struct has no guaranteed layout: the default representation lets the compiler reorder fields and choose padding freely, and that choice can differ across compiler versions, targets, and optimization settings. If a C caller reads the struct by assuming a particular field order and offsets, the moment the layout shifts the foreign side reads garbage, silently, with no type system on the C side to catch it. The layout is an implementation detail that was never promised to anyone, so making it the contract by accident is a latent ABI break waiting on the next rebuild. The two safe alternatives are to pin the layout explicitly with #[repr(C)] so the field order and padding become a stable, documented ABI the C side can rely on, or to drop the struct-as-contract idea entirely and pass an explicit byte buffer with an explicit length whose format you define and document. The dividing line is whether the foreign side wants a stable ABI struct or wants bytes: give it exactly one, documented, and do not let one mechanism pretend to be the other.
